title: LA and Long Beach Port Strike Averted With Tentative Deal
summary: About 250 union watchmen at the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach reached a tentative contract deal on November 21, which takes the strike threat off the table while members vote to ratify it. Here’s what the agreement means for your freight and what to keep an eye on.
body_markdown:
---


Article


**Update, November 21:** The strike threat at Los Angeles and Long Beach is over for now. The Pacific Maritime Association (PMA) said Saturday morning that it reached a tentative agreement with International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILWU) Local 26 after the two sides went back to federally mediated talks on Friday. Local 26 members still have to ratify the deal, and the current contract stays in effect while they vote. Neither side has released the terms, and Local 26 hadn’t commented as of Saturday morning. With the deal in place, terminals and gates should keep running as usual, so you can plan pickups on your normal schedule. Inland rail delays at both ports haven’t gone away, though, so ask your Flexport team how long your rail-bound containers are likely to sit on the terminal. We’ll update this post once Local 26 holds its ratification vote. **Update, November 19:** The Pacific Maritime Association (PMA), which represents the port employers, said on Wednesday that talks with International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILWU) Local 26 ended Tuesday with little movement from the union, and that the union has indicated it won’t extend the contract past 12:01 a.m. Pacific on Saturday, November 21. The two sides plan to meet again on Friday, November 20, so a deal could still happen. If one doesn’t, a strike could start Saturday morning, and the PMA expects other ILWU members to honor the picket lines. If you have freight moving through Los Angeles or Long Beach, ask your Flexport team which terminals your containers are booked through, and we’ll update this post when we know more. Local 26 hadn’t commented when the PMA released its statement, so these details come from the employers.


**Update, November 9:** The strike threat is on hold for now. On Friday, November 6, the PMA and ILWU Local 26 extended their contract through November 20, and the PMA says more talks are scheduled before then. Nothing is settled, and a strike could still start if the extension ends without a deal. The steps below still apply, so keep checking which terminals your containers are booked through.


**Update, November 5:** The strike deadline has moved again. The PMA and ILWU Local 26 have agreed to extend the contract through midnight Pacific on Friday, November 6, and talks will continue on Friday with help from the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service. The PMA says it's still working toward an agreement that avoids disruption at the ports, but nothing is settled. A strike could still start once the extension ends, so the steps below still apply.


**Update, November 4** : About 250 workers could stop container moves at the busiest port complex in the United States as soon as 5 p.m. Pacific today. The International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILWU) Local 26 represents the watchmen who handle gate security and cargo watch at the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach. Its members authorized a strike for Sunday, November 1. On October 30, the union and the Pacific Maritime Association (PMA), which represents the port employers, signed an extension that moved the deadline to 5 p.m. Pacific on Wednesday, November 4. As of Wednesday morning, neither side had announced a deal or another extension. If you have freight moving through either port, find out where it stands this afternoon.


## How 250 workers could impact critical operations


Local 26 members make up about 2% of the ILWU workforce at the two ports. The PMA says they work at six of the complex's 13 container terminals, and those terminals handle about 85% of Long Beach cargo and 33% of Los Angeles cargo. The union's strike notice to other maritime unions lists eight terminal locations:


- APM Terminals (APMT)
- Long Beach Container Terminal (LBCT)
- Total Terminals International (TTI)
- SSA at C-60
- A-90
- LB 206
- Pacific Container Terminal (PCT)
- OH 55


The bigger risk is what the rest of the workforce does. Longshore workers and marine clerks aren't part of this dispute, but the PMA says it doesn't expect them to cross a Local 26 picket line. If they stay off the job, the affected terminals could stop working ships and moving boxes in the yard, and trucks could get turned away at the gates.


## Where the talks stand


Local 26's contract expired in July 2025, and members have worked under extensions since then. The two sides have bargained for more than a year with help from the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service, and Local 26 President Luisa Gratz told other maritime unions on October 23 that those talks had gone nowhere. The PMA says significant differences remain, including on wages. It describes its offer as including wage increases and pension improvements, and it says full-time watchmen already average more than $170,000 a year with employer-paid health care and pensions. Local 26 hasn't published the terms it's seeking.


This dispute is limited to Los Angeles and Long Beach. The coastwide contract that covers about 22,000 longshore workers and clerks at 29 West Coast ports runs through 2028, so Oakland, Seattle, Tacoma and the rest of the coast aren't part of it.


## Why the timing is not optimal


The complex was already stretched before the strike threat. The Port of Los Angeles set an all-time monthly cargo record in September, and the two ports together handle roughly a third of U.S. seaborne container trade. Inland rail hasn't kept up: import containers headed for trains waited an average of 7.19 days on the terminals in September, up from 6.75 days in August, according to the Pacific Merchant Shipping Association. Local trucking gets harder on Saturday, when the California Department of Transportation (Caltrans) closes the Vincent Thomas Bridge for 16 months starting November 7. Retailers are still landing their last holiday inventory, and a shutdown at the gates would hit on top of all of it.


## Questions to ask before 5 p.m. Pacific


Start with where your containers are. Ask your Flexport team which terminal each shipment is booked through, and whether that terminal is one of the locations on the strike notice. A container at a terminal off the list is in a much better position than one on it.


Next, look at timing. For containers that are already available, the question is whether pickup can finish before 5 p.m. Pacific today. For cargo still on the water, ask whether discharge and pickup will land before or after the deadline, and whether a booking that hasn't sailed can shift to a different terminal or another port. Trucks get scarce fast when everyone tries to move freight at once, so ask now.


If a strike does start, plan on delays, and ask how your carrier will handle demurrage and detention (the daily fees for containers left at a terminal or kept past their free time) on boxes you can't reach. Even a short stoppage leaves a line of ships and trucks to clear afterward, and that cleanup can take longer than the strike itself. If it's holiday inventory, give your sales and merchandising teams a heads-up today.


We're watching the talks and will update this post when the PMA or Local 26 announces a deal, another extension or a walkout. The deadline has already moved once, but plan as if this one holds. If you ship through Los Angeles or Long Beach, talk to your Flexport team before 5 p.m. Pacific today.
